title: When a Rival Bids, Your Build Plan Becomes a Buy Decision
documentTitle: Project Liberty — Board Update on Proposed DoubleClick Acquisition (March 23, 2007)
excerptForBlog:
Dear Board Members: I wanted to give you a heads-up about EMG's decision to enter the process to acquire DoubleClick, a leading online ad serving company owned by the private equity firms of Hellman & Friedman and JMI Equity (the transaction is codenamed Project Liberty). As some of you know, we have been interested in this company for some time, but have been pursuing a 'build-it-ourselves' strategy. Our interest became more acute after learning that Microsoft has already made a serious offer. The team believes that this is an important transaction for us, for both offensive and defensive reasons.

We have heard from reliable sources that Microsoft has made a bid in the $1.88 to $2.08 range. This weekend we plan to make a competitive bid by means of a non-binding term sheet/indication of interest.

Google's Rationale for Acquiring DoubleClick: Own DoubleClick's customer footprint to accelerate time to market for our own advertiser and publisher ad serving products. Acquisition of DoubleClick by Microsoft would make it very challenging for us to win customers for our own advertiser ad server, which would impair our opportunities in the brand ad market.

Microsoft's Potential Rationale for Acquiring DoubleClick: Access remnant inventory from DoubleClick's publisher ad server customer base to quickly scale its ad network. Use DoubleClick's advertiser ad server position to harm Yahoo!'s business, driving down its valuation ahead of a potential acquisition.

lessonTitle: When a Rival Bids, Your Build Plan Becomes a Buy Decision
pullQuote: A build-it-yourself plan is only valid until a competitor's checkbook makes the timeline irrelevant.
leadershipTraits: thinks offense and defense at the same time
reads rival motives, not just rival actions
pre-loads the board with logic before the ask
situation: On March 23, 2007, Google's SVP David Drummond sent a brief memo to the board announcing that Google intended to bid for DoubleClick, an ad-serving company owned by two private equity firms. The memo is a weekend heads-up before a non-binding bid goes in. The urgency is explicit: Microsoft has already made a serious offer in the $1.88–$2.08 billion range.
insight: Google had been running a 'build-it-ourselves' strategy on ad serving — and the memo says so plainly. What changed wasn't the value of DoubleClick. What changed was Microsoft's move. The document frames this as both 'offensive and defensive,' but the defensive logic is the sharper one: if Microsoft wins DoubleClick, it gains DoubleClick's advertiser ad server position, which the memo says would 'make it very challenging for us to win customers for our own advertiser ad server.' Build-vs-Buy is usually a cost and speed question. Here it becomes a competitive moat question. Letting a rival acquire the incumbent customer relationships means you're not just building slower — you're building into a wall. The memo also does something unusual: it maps out Microsoft's likely rationale in detail, including using DoubleClick to pressure Yahoo! ahead of a possible acquisition. Google isn't just reacting; it's reading the full board position.
application: If a competitor bids on an asset in your space, don't just ask 'is it worth the price?' Ask what the asset looks like in their hands versus yours. Specifically: does their ownership of it make your organic roadmap harder to execute? If the answer is yes, your build timeline just became a liability. Revisit the decision immediately, with that framing explicit.
